Introduction

St. Maximus is commemorated as Confessor for his defense of Christ's full humanity and divine and human wills. The OCA life describes his education, monastic life, controversy, and suffering. His theology is connected with the Christological curriculum and the history of the sixth ecumenical council. The biographical account and the council's formal definitions remain distinct kinds of source.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

This great man was of a noble family of Constantinople. He became first secretary to the Emperor Heraclius, who prized him much, but he quitted the world and gave himself up to contemplation in a monastery at Chrysopolis, opposite Constantinople. He became abbot there- but seems to have left this retreat on account of its insecurity from hostile attacks. He speaks of the Palestinian ascetic St. Sophronius afterwards Patriarch of Jerusalem, as his master, father, and teacher (Ep. 13), so that he probably passed some time with him, and he was with him in Africa with other monks during the preparations which issued in the "watery union" by which Cyrus the Patriarch reconciled a number of Monophysites to the Church by rejecting the doctrine of "two operations" in Christ (see MONOTHELITISM) .

[2] Historical Roman Catholic biographical reference · Article ‘St. Maximus of Constantinople’; paragraph beginning ‘Known as the Theologian and as Maximus Confessor, born at Constantinop’; bounded selection

Life and notable events

St. Maximus opposed imperial compromise or enforced silence concerning Christ’s wills. The Life describes his debate with Pyrrhus, opposition associated with the Lateran council, arrest, interrogation and exile. His resistance concerned the incarnate Christ’s divine and human willing.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative and concluding account

Pyrrhus thought he might regain his see by the help of the pope. He came to Africa, and in July, 645, a public disputation took place between him and Maximus, in the presence of the Governor Gregory (called George in the MSS. of St. Maximus), who was a friend and correspondent of the saint. The minutes are interesting. Pyrrhus argues that two wills must imply two Persons willing- Maximus replies that in that case there must be three wills in the Holy Trinity. He shows that the will belongs to the Nature, and distinguishes between will as a faculty and will as the act of the faculty. Pyrrhus then admits two wills, on account of the two natures, but adds that we should also confess one will on account of the perfect union. Maximus replies that this would lead us to confess one nature on account of the perfect union. He then cites many passages of Scripture for two wills and two operations. Pyrrhus puts forward Honorius and Vigilius.

[2] Historical Roman Catholic biographical reference · Article ‘St. Maximus of Constantinople’; paragraph beginning ‘Pyrrhus thought he might regain his see by the help of the pope. He ca’; bounded selection

Death and martyrdom

Six years later, in 662, Maximus and the two Anastasii were brought to trial at Constantinople. They were anathematized, and with them St. Martin and St. Sophronius. The prefect was ordered to beat them, to cut out their tongues and lop off their right hands, to exhibit them thus mutilated in every quarter of the city, and to send them to perpetual exile and imprisonment. A long letter of the Roman Anastasius tells us of their sufferings on the journey to Colchis where they were imprisoned in different forts. He tells us that St. Maxirmus foresaw in a vision the day of his death, and that miraculous lights appeared nightly at his tomb. The monk Anastasius had died in the preceding month; the Roman lived on until 666.

[2] Historical Roman Catholic biographical reference · Article ‘St. Maximus of Constantinople’; paragraph beginning ‘Six years later, in 662, Maximus and the two Anastasii were brought to’; bounded selection

Writings and legacy

His legacy includes the Mystagogia, interpretations of difficult patristic passages, and Chapters on Love. The OCA Life connects his later theological influence with St. Symeon the New Theologian and St. Gregory Palamas.
